description: I’m building EarthTrends, an interactive 3D globe that turns 20 years of NASA satellite data into answers anyone can understand: is the climate really changing where you live? I combine GPM IMERG rainfall, MERRA-2 temperature and cloud cover, and GRACE/GRACE-FO water storage with rigorous trend statistics (Mann-Kendall with false-discovery-rate correction) to separate real, sustained change from natural year-to-year noise.
summary:
I built EarthTrends because I kept hearing people say "it rains less than when I was a kid" and I wanted to know if that was actually true.

It's a 3D globe where you can click any place (or search your city) and see 20 years of NASA satellite data for it: rain from GPM, temperature and cloud cover from MERRA-2, and stored water from GRACE. The important part for this challenge is that it doesn't just draw a line. Each place goes through a Mann-Kendall trend test with FDR correction, so the app tells you if there's real evidence of a trend or if it could just be normal year-to-year variation.

You can also compare two places, or let the app find a place changing the opposite way. In Punjab, for example, stored water dropped by about 79 cm (as a layer of water) since 2005, while the Lake Victoria region gained about 111 cm.

It works in English and Spanish, on phone or computer, and you can export all the data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

EarthTrends is a 3D globe where you can click any place on Earth, or search for your city, and see how it changed between 2005 and 2025 using NASA satellite data: yearly rainfall, air temperature, total stored water and how often the sky is clear. Each place gets a short plain-language headline, a chart with one value per year, and a clear label: "Evidence of a long-term trend", "Trend without enough evidence yet" or "No clear trend". There's also a Compare mode to put two places side by side, and a Mirror mode that finds a place on the planet changing the opposite way.

HOW IT WORKS

I downloaded the monthly NASA files (GPM IMERG, MERRA-2 and GRACE/GRACE-FO) and wrote a Python pipeline that turns them into yearly values on a 1° grid. A year only counts if it has at least nine valid months, and missing years stay missing (they are never filled in for the statistics).

Then every grid cell goes through a Mann-Kendall trend test (Hamed-Rao version, which handles years that are correlated with each other), with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction because I'm testing thousands of cells at once. Sen's slope gives the rate of change, and Pettitt's test looks for a possible year when things shifted. The web app only shows the results. It doesn't invent anything, and you can export every series as CSV, JSON or GeoJSON to check it yourself.

WHY IT MATTERS

Everyone has a feeling about how the weather changed where they grew up, but a feeling isn't evidence. The data to check it is free, but hard to use. I first tried NASA's Giovanni, but my requests kept timing out, and even when they work you need to pick datasets, regions and plots, and then interpret the result yourself.

EarthTrends turns that into one tap. You tap your town and see what changed, by how much, and whether there's real evidence behind it, in everyday words. If the evidence isn't strong enough, it says so. Anyone can understand NASA data without a science degree.

WHAT'S CREATIVE ABOUT IT

- Mirror mode: you pick a place and the app finds the strongest opposite trend somewhere else in the world. It makes you see the planet as a connected system.

- A "Stars" layer that turns MERRA-2 cloud cover into clear-sky time and combines it with NASA's Earth at Night image for light pollution.

- A nearby-region comparison, so you can see if your spot is changing more or less than the 500 km around it.

- Every result is written in everyday words, with a simple "i" button that explains each variable.

THINGS I CONSIDERED

- Honesty with the statistics: "significant" never means "100% sure", and "not significant" never means "nothing changed". This is explained in the app.

- GRACE measures broad regions (about 3°) and only over land, so the app shows that and doesn't pretend to have street-level precision.

- It works on phones (portrait and landscape), loads one layer at a time to stay fast, and is available in English and Spanish.

- Accessibility: keyboard shortcuts, keyboard navigation and screen-reader labels.

TOOLS

- Data processing: Python, using libraries to download NASA files (earthaccess), read them (xarray) and run the trend tests (pymannkendall)

- Web app: JavaScript, React, three.js and react-globe.gl

- Hosting: GitHub Pages

- Video: DaVinci Resolve

- AI coding assistants (Claude Code and OpenAI Codex)

AI USE

Code written with help from Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. Data and trend results come from NASA datasets and standard statistical tests, not from AI.
